topic: The Hour-1 Bundle — The Surviving Sepsis Campaign at the Bedside
speakerTitle: Consultant in Emergency & Critical Care Medicine
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Emergency Department & Resuscitation
speakerBio: An emergency and critical-care physician who leads the trust's sepsis-response team. She teaches the golden hour as a choreography — five moves, one clock, no wasted motion.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

The pre-alert crackles in: "62-year-old, query urosepsis, RR 28, BP 84/50, GCS 13, lactate 5.8." The patient rolls through the doors of resus. From this moment a clock is running that you cannot see but every one of the patient's organs can feel. This session is about what your hands must do in the next sixty minutes — the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

In septic shock, time is tissue. The Hour-1 bundle exists because every hour of delay to effective antibiotics measurably raises the chance the patient dies.

2 · From 6 hours to 1 — the evolution of the bundle ⏱️

The original 2004 Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) bundles were split into a 3-hour and a 6-hour bundle. In 2018 the SSC collapsed the initial resuscitation into a single Hour-1 bundle: the elements should be begun immediately, within the first hour of recognition, not spread across a leisurely afternoon. The 2021 guidelines retained this urgency. The word to internalise is "begin" — you are not expected to have completed everything in 60 minutes, but you must have started all of it.

3 · The Hour-1 bundle — the five moves 🖐️

#ElementThe detail that matters
1Measure lactateSend it immediately. Remeasure within 2–4 h if the initial lactate is >2 mmol/L — you are tracking clearance as a resuscitation target.
2Blood cultures BEFORE antibioticsAt least two sets, from separate sites. But: do not let culture-taking delay antibiotics beyond a few minutes. If access is hard, give the drug.
3Broad-spectrum antibioticsEmpiric IV cover for the likely source, ideally within the first hour. In shock, SSC 2021 says give within 1 hour, no delay for investigations.
4IV crystalloid — 30 mL/kgFor hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L. Begin rapidly, complete within ~3 hours. Balanced crystalloid preferred (Session 4).
5VasopressorsIf hypotensive during or after fluid resuscitation, start vasopressors to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. First-line: noradrenaline.
💡 Memory hook — the five fingers

Give three, take two. Give: fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors. Take: lactate, blood cultures. Cultures before antibiotics; lactate remeasured to prove you're winning. Five moves, one hour.

4 · Antibiotics — the single most time-critical act 💊

Of the five, the one with the steepest time–mortality relationship is antibiotics. The landmark data:

  • Kumar et al. (Crit Care Med 2006): in septic shock, each hour of delay to effective antimicrobial therapy after the onset of hypotension was associated with an average ~7.6% increase in mortality. This is the number that built the bundle.
  • Seymour et al. (NEJM 2017): in the New York State mandated-protocol cohort (nearly 50,000 patients), longer time to completion of the 3-hour bundle — and specifically longer time to antibiotics — was associated with higher in-hospital mortality. Notably, faster fluid completion was not as clearly associated, but faster antibiotics was.
  • These data underpin the concept of the "golden hour" of sepsis: the earlier effective cover reaches the bloodstream, the better the odds.
🎯 Nuance — shock vs sepsis-without-shock

SSC 2021 stratifies the antibiotic recommendation. For septic shock or high-probability sepsis: antibiotics immediately, within 1 hour — the evidence is strong and delay is lethal. For possible sepsis without shock: a short period of rapid investigation is permitted (up to ~3 hours) to decide whether infection is really the cause, because reflexively broad-spectrum-dosing every uncertain patient drives resistance and harm. The sicker the patient, the less you get to think.

5 · Blood cultures before antibiotics — but never a delay 🧫

Why cultures first? Because a single dose of antibiotic can sterilise the blood within minutes to a couple of hours, and a negative culture then robs you of the chance to de-escalate to a narrow, targeted agent later — prolonging broad-spectrum exposure, toxicity, and resistance. So the rule is: two sets, separate sites, then the drug. The hard clinical judgement is the timing trade-off — if obtaining cultures will take more than a few minutes (difficult access in a shocked patient), the antibiotic wins. A missed culture is recoverable; a delayed antibiotic in shock may not be.

6 · Fluids & pressors in the bundle 💧

The bundle's circulatory arm is deliberately blunt to be fast: 30 mL/kg of crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4, begun immediately. This is a starting dose, not a ceiling or a mandate to ignore the individual patient — Session 4 is entirely about what happens next (dynamic reassessment, when to stop). If the patient remains hypotensive during or after that fluid, do not keep chasing with more litres — start noradrenaline to defend a MAP ≥65 mmHg. Early vasopressor, even before fluids are "finished," is legitimate and often kidney-protective in profound shock.

💡 Pearl — MAP 65 is the floor, not the goal

Targeting a MAP of 65 mmHg is the default. Higher targets (e.g. 80–85) did not improve mortality overall in the SEPSISPAM trial and caused more atrial fibrillation — though chronically hypertensive patients had less renal injury at the higher target. Default to 65; individualise upward only with reason.

7 · Bundle compliance and mortality — does the checklist actually work? ✅

Yes — and this is the strongest argument for the whole approach. Beyond Seymour's New York data, multiple large quality-improvement programmes have shown that rising bundle compliance tracks with falling sepsis mortality. The SSC's own performance-improvement cohorts demonstrated that hospitals which improved adherence to measuring lactate, drawing cultures, and delivering timely antibiotics and fluids saw absolute mortality reductions. The bundle is not magic — it is simply a forcing function that makes the reliable delivery of time-critical basics the default rather than a matter of luck and memory at 3 a.m.

8 · Source control — the element people forget 🔪

Antibiotics cannot cure an abscess, an obstructed infected kidney, an empyema, dead bowel, or an infected line. SSC 2021 recommends identifying and controlling the source as rapidly as feasible — ideally within 6–12 hours of diagnosis where anatomically achievable: drain the collection, relieve the obstruction, remove the device, debride the necrosis. A perfectly delivered Hour-1 bundle around an undrained source is a holding manoeuvre, not a cure.

☠️ M&M — "We were waiting for the cultures"

A 45-year-old man with meningococcaemia arrived at 22:10 — purpuric rash, RR 30, BP 82/44, lactate 6. Peripheral access failed twice, so the team pressed on trying to obtain blood cultures and a second cannula before giving antibiotics "to do it properly." Ceftriaxone was not delivered until 23:35 — 85 minutes after arrival. He deteriorated into refractory shock and DIC and died the next morning. At review, the delay to antibiotics was judged the key modifiable failure: guidance is explicit that in septic shock, if cultures cannot be obtained promptly, the antibiotic must not wait. Lesson: cultures-before-antibiotics is a rule about sequence when it costs nothing, not a licence to delay the drug. In shock, the golden hour outranks a perfect microbiology work-up. An intraosseous needle and immediate ceftriaxone would have been the right call within minutes.

9 · A time-anchored walkthrough of the golden hour ⏳

  1. 0 min — Recognise & escalate. Sepsis screen positive, senior and critical-care alerted. Oxygen on, two large-bore cannulae.
  2. 0–10 min — Take two. Blood cultures ×2 and a venous/arterial lactate drawn with the same access. Bloods including FBC, U&E, LFT, clotting, CRP.
  3. 10–20 min — Give the drug. Empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotic for the likely source running. In shock, this is the priority act.
  4. 0–60 min — Fill the tank. Start 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension/lactate ≥4.
  5. During/after fluids — Defend the pressure. Persistent MAP <65 → noradrenaline via best available access; escalate to central line and arterial line.
  6. 2–4 h — Prove you're winning. Remeasure lactate; reassess perfusion; plan source control and de-escalation.

10 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Hour-1 bundle = give three, take two: fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors; lactate, cultures.
  • Antibiotics are the most time-critical act — Kumar's ~7.6%/hour, Seymour's mandated-cohort data. In shock: within 1 hour.
  • Cultures before antibiotics — but never delay the drug in shock for the sake of a culture.
  • 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4; noradrenaline to MAP ≥65 if still hypotensive.
  • Remeasure lactate to confirm resuscitation is working.
  • Source control within 6–12 h — antibiotics cannot cure undrained pus.
  • Compliance saves lives: the bundle is a forcing function for reliable basics.

Next session: we take the blunt 30 mL/kg starting point apart — how much fluid, which fluid, and the far harder skill of knowing when to stop.

moderatorQs.q: The bundle says take blood cultures before antibiotics. In a patient in septic shock with impossible venous access, how do you resolve that tension?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: You resolve it firmly in favour of the antibiotic. Cultures-before-antibiotics is a rule about sequence when it costs no meaningful time — its purpose is to preserve the ability to de-escalate later, not to gate the life-saving drug. SSC 2021 is explicit that in septic shock antibiotics should be given within one hour and must not be delayed to obtain cultures if access is difficult. Practically: make one quick, competent attempt at two culture sets; if that fails, place an intraosseous needle and give empiric broad-spectrum cover immediately, taking cultures as soon as access is subsequently secured. A missed culture is recoverable; each hour of delayed antibiotics in shock carries roughly a 7–8% absolute mortality cost (Kumar 2006).

moderatorQs.q: Why did SSC 2021 introduce a distinction between 'septic shock' and 'possible sepsis without shock' for antibiotic timing?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the evidence for immediacy is strongest where the risk is highest, and reflexive broad-spectrum dosing of every uncertain patient carries its own harms. For septic shock or high-probability sepsis, delay is clearly lethal, so the recommendation is antibiotics within 1 hour, no waiting for work-up. For possible sepsis without shock, the guideline permits a brief window of rapid assessment (up to ~3 hours) to decide whether infection is genuinely the cause — because inappropriately treating non-infective mimics drives antimicrobial resistance, C. difficile, and drug toxicity without benefit. The principle: the sicker and more certain the patient, the less time you take; the more diagnostic doubt and the more stable the patient, the more it is legitimate to investigate first.

moderatorQs.q: A junior asks whether targeting a MAP of 65 is too low for an elderly hypertensive patient. What does the evidence say?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Default to MAP ≥65 mmHg — that is the SSC target and the level at which the SEPSISPAM trial found no overall mortality benefit from aiming higher (80–85 mmHg), while the higher target caused more atrial fibrillation. So a higher pressure is not free. However, SEPSISPAM did show that patients with chronic hypertension randomised to the higher target needed less renal replacement therapy, suggesting their autoregulatory curve is shifted. The pragmatic answer: start at 65 for everyone, and in a chronically hypertensive patient with ongoing renal hypoperfusion consider individualising the target modestly upward, weighing the arrhythmia risk. Sixty-five is the floor and the default, not a dogma.

audienceQs.q: The bundle is called 'Hour-1' — does that mean everything must be finished within 60 minutes?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Not finished — begun. The 2018/2021 SSC deliberately uses the word 'begin': all five elements should be initiated within the first hour of recognition. Realistically, cultures and lactate are drawn and antibiotics started within that hour, while the 30 mL/kg fluid bolus is begun immediately but may take up to about 3 hours to run in, and lactate is remeasured at 2–4 hours. The spirit is urgency without waiting for perfection: never let a pending investigation stall an antibiotic or a fluid start. Think 'start the clock, start everything,' not 'complete everything by minute 60.'

audienceQs.q: Why do we insist on cultures before antibiotics if it risks delaying treatment?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because a single antibiotic dose can sterilise the blood within minutes to a couple of hours, and once the cultures turn negative you lose the ability to identify the organism and its sensitivities. That costs you the chance to de-escalate from broad empirical cover to a narrow, targeted agent — prolonging broad-spectrum exposure, toxicity, C. difficile risk and resistance. So when it costs essentially no time, we draw two sets first. The crucial caveat: this is a sequencing rule, not a delay rule. In septic shock, if cultures can't be obtained promptly, the antibiotic goes in first and cultures follow once access allows.

audienceQs.q: If the patient is still hypotensive after 30 mL/kg, do I give more fluid or start noradrenaline?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Start noradrenaline and stop reflexively chasing with more litres. The bundle says vasopressors for hypotension during or after fluid resuscitation to defend a MAP ≥65 — and there is good rationale for early vasopressor rather than escalating fluid, because ongoing large-volume resuscitation worsens the capillary leak and tissue oedema of sepsis (Session 4) and delays perfusion restoration. Before giving any further bolus, prove the patient is still fluid-responsive with a dynamic test — passive leg raise, stroke-volume variation, or IVC/echo assessment. If they are not fluid-responsive, more fluid only causes harm; the pressor is the correct next move. Noradrenaline is first-line, titrated to MAP 65, ideally via central access but peripherally in the interim if needed.
